 UPDATE: 2026/10/31 11:00 EST BY SEAN MCMANUS
 Ford Once Built One Of The Most Reliable Trucks Ever 
 We added a section to discuss Ford's old F-250 with its unkillable 7.3-liter PowerStroke V8 turbodiesel.
 Ford has an image problem right now, mainly due to its poor recall record over the past couple of years. In 2025, Ford launched 153 recall campaigns in the US, affecting almost 13 million vehicles and setting an industry record. Yet, it seems like a regular occurrence for a new Ford recall to be reported. In the past few days, the Ford F-150 had three recalls issued for issues including the tailgate, speedometer, and tachometer. Even Ford's Godzilla engine is having a nightmare right now.

 Ford is, of course, aware of the recalls and needs to protect the Ford F-Series truck's dominant sales – and it has a plan that will fix reliability for its next-gen F-150.
 Ford Is Increasing Its Endurance Testing And Test Mileage
 While Ford's CEO, Jim Farley, didn't expressly talk about the recalls, during Ford's Q3 conference call it became clear the next-generation F-150 is being set up to be the new standard in reliability and durability. But not just the F-150 – the plan is to spread the new approach across the company.
 “Prototypes begin, builds are beginning in first quarter 2027, just a couple months away. We have an incredible powertrain durability testing, which is now five-fold increase, to meet our bulletproof powertrain target at Ford. We’re doubling endurance and strength-testing, and increasing full-vehicle test mileage by nearly 60%, to almost 4 million miles. The F-150 will be the most extensively tested truck ever at Ford, and we will apply this exact same approach across our company.”
 – Ford CEO, Jim Farley.
 Those are big numbers when it comes to testing, increasing full-vehicle test miles from 1.6 million to four million miles. And expensive when stretching out endurance and strength testing as well.
 Is It Possible To Build Modern Bulletproof Powertrains?
 2022 Ford F-150 Lightning testing in Alaska Ford 
 Complexity has been the enemy of durability since the dawn of engineering. Engines now have to be complex to meet all kinds of standards when it comes to fuel economy and emissions while also generating enough power. The problem for Ford will be that complexity and bulletproof reliability must also be balanced against the need to keep material and production costs down and, ultimately, continue to make a profit.
 Even Toyota, the king of reliable vehicles, has had trouble with the complexity vs. reliability problem when it comes to a full-size pickup truck . But that doesn't mean it can't be done. Ford has been building truck engines for a long time, and there's a reason that the F-Series pickup trucks have been untouchable in sales charts since the 1970s.
 Ford Once Built One Of The Most Reliable Trucks Ever
 2003 Ford F-250 front 3/4 high angle in white while parked Bring A Trailer 
 Ford might be having quality control issues today, but it wasn't always that way. In fact, the automaker once offered a truck that could regularly reach 400,000+ miles: the late ninth-gen F-250 and early first-gen Super Duty models. F-250s from 1994.5 through 1997 and Super Duty models from 1999 through 2003 equipped with Ford's 7.3-liter PowerStroke V8 turbo-diesel are virtually unkillable.
 While modern diesel engines are restricted by emissions equipment, this old 7.3L lacks any form of particulate filters or exhaust fluid systems. It's not perfect, though. One main failure point of this engine is its camshaft position sensor, but even that part is cheap and easy enough to replace on the side of the road if needed.
 CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters
 Hopefully, Ford can bring about a return to form and build trucks that aren't constantly being recalled. There's always the threat of Toyota gaining ground and building trucks that can pull Ford customers away in meaningful numbers. In the pickup truck market, durability is everything, particularly when it comes to fleet vehicles where time is money. A company having to pull all of its trucks out of service for a few hours to have a recall issue fixed is a problem.
 If Ford does this right, though, it could set the new truck drivetrain standard for durability.
